claims.text: Conventionally cast bulk W-based refractory HEAs have a coarse-grained microstructure.
W-Ta-Cr-V refractory HEAs can contain Cr- and V-rich precipitates that may embrittle the alloy.
Equal-channel angular pressing or high-pressure torsion can convert the proposed bulk refractory HEA into a controlled, stable nanocrystalline state.
Nanocrystalline W-based refractory HEAs can remain thermally and irradiation stable under heavy-ion irradiation, dual-beam irradiation, and helium implantation.
Nanocrystalline refractory HEA structures can withstand exposure at approximately 1100 °C for several days.
Refining the alloy to nanocrystalline grain sizes increases its grain-boundary density.
The increased grain-boundary density creates effective barriers to dislocation motion.
The increased grain-boundary density provides sinks for radiation-induced defects.
Nanocrystalline refractory HEAs can generate and evolve relatively few irradiation defects and can exhibit no detectable irradiation-induced grain growth.
Grain refinement strengthens refractory HEAs through the Hall-Petch mechanism.
Nanocrystalline grain refinement improves both yield strength and ductility relative to bulk refractory HEAs.
Severe-plastic-deformation-processed bulk refractory HEAs will retain improved strength and ductility after combined high-temperature and irradiation exposure.
The nanocrystalline alloy will exhibit a 50–100% increase in yield strength relative to a conventionally cast coarse-grained baseline.
The nanocrystalline alloy will undergo minimal grain growth or new-phase formation during prolonged high-temperature and irradiation exposure.
Conventional refractory HEAs commonly have limited room-temperature ductility and formability.
Precipitates in W-Ta-Cr-V alloys may be detrimental to mechanical properties through embrittlement.
Temperatures well above 1100 °C or extremely aggressive irradiation doses may cause grain growth or phase evolution that eliminates the mechanical benefit.
